The query “roger federer” is not a request for any page that contains “roger” and “federer”: a marathon result list with a Roger in row 12 and a Federer in row 4,000 matches both terms but answers nothing. In

we added frequent phrases such as “New York City” to the vocabulary as n-grams. That works for a fixed list of known phrases, but it cannot adapt to the new names and phrases that appear with every news event. Names matter a lot on the web, since people, places, and products are among the most frequent search topics. We therefore want a proximity measure that works for any combination of query terms and is computed at query time.
The index provides the raw material. Instead of storing only the term frequency in a posting, a
stores every position at which the term occurs in the document. This list is called a

children.value: The article writes the full name only twice: in its first words, “Roger Federer (born 8 August 1981) is a Swiss former professional tennis player”, and near the end, in “the Roger Federer Foundation”. In between, it follows the usual style and refers to him by his surname alone.

At query time, we pair up occurrences of the two terms. The full cross product would create 30 pairs, most of them meaningless: “roger” at position 1 and “federer” at position 619 are more than 600 words apart. Instead, we merge both hit lists into one list sorted by position and form a pair wherever two neighbouring entries belong to different terms (Büttcher, Clarke, and Lushman; see the Further Reading section of the chapter summary). The merged list starts with roger (1), federer (2), federer (57) and ends with federer (509), roger (532), federer (533), federer (560), federer (619).

This gives three pairs: (1, 2), (509, 532), and (532, 533); position 532 belongs to two of them. The thirteen surname-only mentions in between form no pair, since a pair needs both terms. The pair (509, 532) is in reversed order and links the end of one mention to the start of the next: “Federer played an instrumental role in the creation of the Laver Cup team competition. He is also an active philanthropist, having established the Roger”. The rule treats both query terms alike, needs no window size, and works unchanged for queries with more than two terms.

Now take a marathon result list of 5,000 runners: a long table of ranks, names, and finishing times. Six runners have the first name Roger and six the surname Federer, among them a Roger in row 12 and a Federer in row 4,000. By term counts, the list is a serious candidate: it contains “roger” three times as often as the article. Merging the hit lists gives 11 pairs, more than the article’s 3. But every pair joins two different runners hundreds of rows apart, all pairs drop out of the bins, and the list scores 0. Proximity pushes the article above the list.

The idea stays the same: the closer the query terms appear, the more likely the page is about the combination and not just about each term on its own. Proximity has a storage price. The postings lists of

store only the documents that contain a term; a positional index adds every position of the term and is therefore considerably larger. Web search engines pay this price, because the same positions also answer phrase queries such as “new york city” without indexing every n-gram.

The page contains “university” nine times. Grouped by tag, we get one occurrence in the title, two in

headings, two in bold text, three in paragraphs, and one in a link. A natural first idea is to saturate the count in each tag separately, as BM25 does for the whole document, and then add up the weighted results. This idea is flawed. If every field saturates on its own, a spammer can repeat a keyword in the title, in every heading, in bold text, and in the body, and collect the full saturated score once per field. The combination grows almost linearly with the number of fields, and the protection that saturation was meant to provide is gone.
(BM25 with fields) does it the other way around. It first combines the per-field counts into one weighted term frequency and only then applies the BM25 saturation:

Saturation matters more on the web than in a curated collection, because keyword stuffing is a standard SEO technique (
). Field weighting also extends beyond HTML tags: the URL, the domain name, and the anchor texts of incoming links (next subsection) are all fields with their own weights.

The anchor text of a link is the clickable text that leads to another page. It usually describes the target page in a few precise words, chosen not by the target’s author but by someone else. Generic anchors such as “click here” or “more” carry no information, but with thousands of links to a page the useful descriptions dominate.

Anchor text is valuable because it is hard to manipulate. A page author controls every word on their own page, but not the words that thousands of other sites use to link to it. Anchor text also describes pages that contain little text of their own, such as a home page made of images and navigation menus, and it can even describe pages the crawler has never fetched.
Using anchor text requires work at crawl time. When the crawler parses a page, it extracts each link together with its anchor text and stores the pair under the
). After the crawl, the search engine builds a separate

in which each target page is described by the concatenation of all anchor texts pointing to it. At query time, the anchor index contributes its own score, usually with a higher weight than the page’s own text.

The saturation for anchor counts must be gentler than BM25’s. Many independent pages voting for a description is exactly the evidence we want, so the score should keep growing with the number of votes, only more slowly. A logarithm such as

Many queries have a local intent that the user does not spell out. Someone typing “best pizza” on a phone in Basel wants a restaurant within walking distance, not the best pizzeria in Naples. Google introduced a major local-search update, nicknamed Pigeon, in 2014, which tied local results more closely to the user’s location and to the distance to businesses. Today, location influences the ranking of restaurants, shops, services, events, and many general queries.
Location-aware ranking needs three pieces of information:

For businesses, the owners often maintain an entry with address and opening hours in a directory such as Google Maps, so the search engine knows the location exactly. For other pages, the crawler estimates a location from the address on the page, the country domain, or the server’s IP address.

The device may report its GPS position. Otherwise the search engine estimates the location from the IP address, which fails when the user connects through a VPN. If the query names a place, that place takes precedence: “best pizza in Paris” ranks Paris restaurants, even for a user in Basel. The query analyzer recognizes places as named entities (
) and maps them to coordinates. This works for landmarks too, as in “best pizza near the Golden Gate Bridge”.
How much location matters for this query.
“best pizza” depends strongly on location. “Albert Einstein” is a global query, but a local museum with an Einstein exhibition can still receive a modest local boost.

A user who asks for a recipe in German does not want English pages, even if an English page matches the query terms well. Language is therefore a signal of its own. The search engine detects the language of each page at indexing time, with the same classifiers that detect the language of a query (
). On the user side, the language of the query, the interface language, the browser settings, and past queries indicate which languages the user reads.

The engine can use this signal in two ways. A classical filter restricts the results to pages in the user’s languages, like the language option of an advanced search form. A filter is simple, but it is all or nothing: it also removes an English page that would be the best result when no good German page exists. Learning to rank (

) instead treats the language match as one feature among many and learns from user behaviour how strongly to prefer pages in the query language. A recipe query then shows German pages first, while a query for an error message of a programming framework may still rank English pages high, because that is where the answers are.

described the kinds of low-quality content on the web, from outdated pages to scams and pages that exist only to rank. Search engines respond by estimating the quality of each page and the trustworthiness of its site. Typical measures include:
for low-quality pages: thin content that wraps a few sentences in ads, pages copied from elsewhere, aggressive keyword stuffing, and clickbait whose content does not deliver what the title promises.
of entire sites from the results: link farms that exist only to create links, doorway pages that redirect users elsewhere, malware sites, and illegal content.

: signals such as the known ownership of a site, its age, its editorial quality, and its reputation in other sources. A registered news organization or a university earns more trust than an anonymous site created last week.

Quality updates can shift results on a large scale. Google’s 2011 Panda update, which targeted thin and low-quality content, noticeably affected about 12% of US English queries. Since then, quality assessment has moved to machine-learned classifiers. Google uses a spam detection system called SpamBrain, and its human quality raters judge pages by experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness (E-E-A-T); their judgments become training labels for the ranking models (
). Since 2023, large amounts of cheap, machine-generated text have made this defence harder and more important.

Quality signals have a cost. A ranking that rewards established, trusted sites makes it harder for a new site to reach the top, even if its content is excellent. Search engines therefore balance trust against freshness and diversity, a trade-off we meet again in
